title: 'I Can't Do This, I Wasn't Here Last Lesson' - Absence, Lessons and Learning lessons-and-learning/
author: D. Cox
summary: Writing against DfE data showing persistent absence at 20% for the year, RE teacher D. Cox sets out three curriculum-design strategies she uses to stop intermittent absence from becoming a total content gap for individual students. Her first move is structural: rather than planning a scheme of work by lesson, where missing one lesson means missing that topic entirely, she teaches by topic across lessons, spreading the same topic across multiple sessions so an absent student still gets partial exposure to everything rather than a total blank on whatever they missed. Her second strategy uses repeated starter questions - the same specific recall question, such as where a religious dialogue took place, asked across several consecutive lessons - so that even students who weren't present for the original teaching absorb the key fact through sheer repetition in starters and answer reviews. Her third strategy, aimed particularly at longer humanities topics, builds lessons around a single overarching enquiry question that each session contributes a case study toward, so a student who attended only two of ten lessons still has two genuine, partial answers to draw on rather than nothing. She's careful to note these strategies target the common pattern of intermittent attenders rather than chronic school-refusers, and that the same techniques strengthen retention for the whole class, not just those who are frequently absent.
points: Cox's central structural fix is teaching "by topic across lessons" rather than "by lesson," so a student who misses one lesson still gets partial exposure to every topic rather than zero exposure to whichever lessons they missed.

Her repeated-starter-question technique deliberately reuses the same retrieval question across consecutive lessons so absent students absorb key content passively through repetition even without having been taught it directly.

Her long-term enquiry question structure gives students a stable anchor they can answer from partial attendance, since each lesson contributes one of several possible supporting case studies rather than a single cumulative thread.

She's explicit that these strategies aren't aimed at chronic school-refusers but at the more common pattern of students who attend intermittently, and that the same techniques benefit the whole class, not just persistently absent students.
quotes: The DfE data on absence isn’t a happy read. With persistent absence at 20% for the academic year so far, it’s clear that we are dealing with an issue that there are no silver bullets for.
So I don’t teach ‘by lesson’, I teach by topic across lessons.

When I start the lesson we always do a re-cap of the last lesson so all students can get back into things. This places the learning into context for the absent student and they can see last lesson’s notes on the screen via my visualiser.
For example, at the start of the topic on Hindus teachings on life after death we talk about the story of Krishna and Arjuna being on a battlefield when discussing issues of life and death.

For the following lessons, I ask the starter question ‘Where were Arjuna and Krishna when they had the conversation?’ After a few lessons, students that weren’t in the initial lesson know it was on a battlefield because we repeatedly reference it.
A student can have missed a few lessons but can still answer the question from the two lessons they attended because in those two lessons they have two possible answers to the question.

These three strategies mean that I don't have students sitting wasting even more time in class saying 'I don't know about this' or when it is summative assessment time, not being able to write anything.
